The closest direct evidence is [Recency Sampling (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02643), which applies recency-biased supervision to GRU4Rec and other sequential recommenders; it supports testing recency emphasis, not a universally optimal exponential decay. Searches found no directly matching 2024–2026 study establishing the proposed gradient diagnostics for GRU4Rec. The [original implementation](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec) also distinguishes session-based training from personalized sequences requiring backpropagation through time. Verify the actual training graph before interpreting temporal credit assignment.

A diagnostic proposal, extrapolating from [gradient-conflict research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.06782): on the same trained network, compute unweighted per-position parameter gradients g_t=∇θℓ_t, their norms, and cosine alignment between older and recent supervision, separately for recurrent parameters and embeddings. For normalized exponential weights, the training gradient is Σw_tg_t/Σw_t; compare its direction and older-position contribution against uniform weighting. Negative alignment indicates local conflict, but does not establish that older supervision harms validation performance. Mask padding and index positions relative to each sequence’s final valid item.

Report [weight-concentration ESS](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.03572), (Σw)²/Σw², alongside valid-target count; correlated sequence positions mean this is not an independent-sample count. Probe recurrent memory separately through final-loss gradients to earlier hidden states/input embeddings and lag-wise history perturbations. [RNN gradient analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.5063) explains attenuation through recurrent Jacobian products; perturbation sensitivity measures current dependence, not the usefulness of older training targets. Stronger decay therefore needs controlled macro validation HR@10 improvement, supported by gradient alignment and acceptable supervision concentration.
